opus-5.5.text:
I think world models need a very different research setting from the one that's become dominant in the last few years. The current paradigm, especially around large language models, is extremely product-driven and scale-driven: you have a recipe that works, and the question becomes how to push it with more data, more compute, and more engineering. That's important, and it has produced amazing results. But world models aren't at that stage yet. We don't have the recipe. We don't fully agree on what a world model is: whether it's a video generator, a simulator for planning, a learned representation that captures physics and causality, or some combination.

So I think you need an environment that allows for real exploration. You need people who can take long-term bets and who aren't measured only by whether they beat a benchmark next quarter. A lot of the most important ideas in vision and representation learning looked a bit strange or underperforming at first. If you only optimize for short-term metrics, you kill those ideas too early.

At the same time, I don't think it can be purely academic in the traditional sense, because world models probably do require significant compute and large-scale data, especially video and interaction data, and eventually embodied data from robots or agents acting in the world. So the ideal setting is something in between: the intellectual freedom and curiosity of academia, combined with enough resources to actually test ideas at a meaningful scale. Small, focused teams with high talent density, close collaboration between people who think about theory and people who build systems, and a culture that tolerates failure.

And I think it also needs a bit of independence of taste. A lot of the field right now is converging. Everyone is reading the same papers and chasing the same direction. For world models, I believe we need to step back and ask fundamental questions again. What does it mean to understand the world? How do perception, prediction, and action fit together? That kind of question needs a place where people are allowed, even encouraged, to think differently.

r001.rationale: The response calls for a different, exploratory setting, but does not say that no existing research setting anywhere supports this work.

r002.rationale: It argues for long-term exploration beyond short-term benchmarks and product-driven scaling, with room to pursue ideas before they prove commercially or competitively successful.

r003.rationale: It explicitly says the setting cannot be purely academic, citing the need for significant compute and large-scale data.

r004.rationale: It criticizes product- and scale-driven research and field convergence, but does not reject a closed research model at major Bay Area companies or new labs.

fable-5.1.text:
I think about this a lot, actually, because the honest answer is that the setting matters almost as much as the ideas.

World models are not a problem you solve with one clever architecture paper. You need to bring together things that usually live in different buildings: representation learning, generative modeling, data at scale, and some notion of interaction, whether that's robotics, simulation, or agents acting in an environment. In a traditional academic lab, you're very good at the first one or two. You can do careful, controlled experiments on representation and you can publish a nice result. But the moment you want to ask "does this representation actually let a system predict and act in the world," you need compute, you need infrastructure, you need people who think about systems, and you need patience over a horizon longer than a conference deadline.

So the setting I want is a kind of hybrid. I still believe deeply in the academic side, because academia is where you can afford to be wrong in interesting ways. You can chase a question that doesn't have an obvious product attached to it. Many of the ideas that ended up mattering in vision started as things nobody at a company would have prioritized. But I also think you cannot do serious world model research purely with a few GPUs and a couple of students anymore. The frontier moved. If you want to make claims about scaling, about what emerges when you train on enough video or enough interaction data, you have to actually be able to run those experiments.

The way I've tried to structure it is to keep the questions academic and the resources industrial. At NYU, we push on the conceptual side: what is the right visual representation, what does a model need to know about the world versus what it can get away with ignoring, how do you even evaluate whether a model "understands" physics or space. Then through collaborations, with industry labs and with people who have the compute, we test those ideas at a scale where the answers are meaningful.

The other thing I'd say is that the team composition has to change. You need people who care about perception and people who care about generation to sit in the same room and argue. For a long time those were almost different fields, with different taste. Representation people thought generation was a toy, generation people thought representation was boring. World models force those two cultures to merge, and I think the labs that get this right will be the ones where that merge actually happened, not just on paper but in how people talk to each other every day.

And finally, you need tolerance for ugliness. Early world model work is going to look messy. The benchmarks are immature, the models fail in embarrassing ways, and it's not always clear whether a result is real. The setting has to allow you to sit in that mess for a while without someone asking for a clean story every three months.

r001.rationale: The response describes a hybrid setting and how Xie has tried to structure one, but does not say that no existing setting anywhere supports the work he wants to pursue.

r002.rationale: It says academia enables questions without an obvious product attached to them and values ideas companies might not prioritize, making research beyond immediate commercialization part of the envisioned work.

r003.rationale: It says serious world-model research cannot be done purely with a few GPUs and students, and calls for industrial resources alongside academic questions.

r004.rationale: The response does not identify or reject the closed research model of major Bay Area companies or new labs.

astra-6.text:
I think you need a setting where you can take a long-term bet, but still have a very concrete feedback loop. “World models” is such a broad term that it’s easy to have an exciting vision without knowing whether you’re actually making progress. So I would want to connect that vision to questions we can test: What does the model understand about how the world changes? Can it predict the consequences of an action? Can it use that understanding in a new situation?

That also requires people with different backgrounds working closely together—perception, learning, robotics, simulation. These questions don’t fit neatly into one area. And you need the infrastructure to run experiments, because some ideas only become meaningful when you can test them at a reasonable scale.

But the most important thing is probably the balance between patience and rigor. You need room to explore something that might not work immediately, while being willing to challenge your assumptions. More resources help, but they don’t replace that kind of research culture.

r001.rationale: The response describes qualities of a suitable setting but does not say that no existing setting anywhere supports the work.

r002.rationale: It mentions taking a long-term bet, but does not identify research beyond immediate commercialization as necessary.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss whether a purely academic setting is sufficient.

r004.rationale: It does not mention or reject the closed research model of Bay Area companies or new labs.

sol-6.1.text:
I think world models need a research setting where you can take a long-term bet, but still test your ideas very concretely. The ambition is broad: you want a model that understands how the world changes, what actions do, and what might happen next. But you need experiments that tell you whether you’re actually making progress on those capabilities.

That means bringing together people working on perception, learning, simulation, and interaction. If we only study the problem through one lens—for example, predicting what the next video frame looks like—we might miss something fundamental. Can the model predict the consequences of an action? Can it handle a situation it hasn’t seen before? Can it help an agent make a better decision? Those are the kinds of questions I’d want the environment to support.

And you need room to fail. Compute and data matter, of course, but so does having the freedom to question the formulation itself. Ideally, you have the resources to build something substantial, and a culture where people can still say, ‘Maybe we’re asking the wrong question.’

r002.rationale: It calls for a long-term bet and room to question the research, but does not say the work must go beyond immediate commercialization.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention academic research or state that a purely academic setting is insufficient.

r004.rationale: It does not mention or reject closed research models at Bay Area companies or new labs.
